summary: Specifies LISP-SEC, a set of security mechanisms giving origin authentication, integrity, and anti-replay protection to the mapping data returned in LISP lookups. It also lets a requester verify authorization for EID-prefix claims in Map-Reply messages. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: LISP splits an address into a part that identifies the endpoint and a part that says where to reach it, and looks the second part up when traffic is sent. RFC 9303 makes that lookup trustworthy: the requester and the servers involved agree on a key for that one lookup, and each of them signs what they send, so a fake or altered answer is rejected.

questions: how to secure lisp mapping lookups
how does lisp-sec protect map-reply messages
what is a one-time key in lisp
subtitle: Adds one-time keys and HMACs to LISP map lookups so a forged or overclaimed mapping gets caught.

tldr.problem: LISP looks up where an endpoint lives with Map-Request and Map-Reply messages. If a Map-Reply is not protected against tampering, an attacker can change it to hijack traffic, impersonate an endpoint, or overclaim an EID-Prefix.
tldr.mechanism: For each Map-Request the ingress tunnel router makes a fresh one-time key. The Map-Server uses it to sign the EID-Prefix it authorizes and derives a second key for the egress tunnel router, which signs the whole Map-Reply. The ingress tunnel router checks both signatures.
tldr.outcome: The ingress tunnel router gets origin authentication, integrity and anti-replay protection for the mapping data, and can reject records for prefixes the Map-Server never authorized.

today: RFC 9303 is a Proposed Standard, published in October 2022. No RFC obsoletes it and no RFC updates it. It builds on the LISP specifications in RFC 9300 and RFC 9301.

sections.title: Securing LISP Mapping Lookups
sections.content:
The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) is a network-layer protocol that separates IP addresses into two numbering spaces, Endpoint Identifiers and Routing Locators. EID-to-RLOC mappings are stored in a database and in the LISP Mapping System, and are made available through the Map-Request and Map-Reply lookup process. If these mappings, carried in Map-Reply messages, are transmitted without integrity protection, an adversary can manipulate them and hijack the communication, impersonate the requested EID, or mount denial-of-service attacks. Also, if the Map-Reply is transported unauthenticated, an adversarial LISP entity can overclaim an EID-Prefix and maliciously redirect traffic. The LISP-SEC threat model is built on top of the LISP threat model of RFC 7835, which includes a detailed description of the overclaiming attack.

This memo specifies LISP-SEC, a set of security mechanisms that provides origin authentication, integrity and anti-replay protection to LISP's EID-to-RLOC mapping data conveyed through the mapping lookup process. LISP-SEC also enables verification of authorization on EID-Prefix claims in Map-Reply messages: it ensures that the sender of a Map-Reply giving the location for an EID-Prefix is entitled to do so according to the EID-Prefix registered with the associated Map-Server.

Map-Register and Map-Notify security, including the right of a LISP entity to register an EID-Prefix or to claim presence at an RLOC, is out of the scope of LISP-SEC, because those protocols are protected by the security mechanisms specified in RFC 9301. LISP-SEC does, however, extend the Map-Register message to let an ingress tunnel router downgrade to non-LISP-SEC Map-Requests.
sections.plainLanguage: When a LISP router needs to know where to send a packet, it asks for the location of the destination and gets an answer back. Without protection, anyone able to touch that exchange can change the answer and send the traffic somewhere else, or answer for an address range they do not own. LISP-SEC makes each exchange verifiable.

sections.title: The Terms LISP-SEC Introduces
sections.content:
The document defines a small set of terms. The One-Time Key is an ephemeral, randomly generated key that must be used for a single Map-Request and Map-Reply exchange. The ITR One-Time Key is the one generated at the Ingress Tunnel Router, and the MS One-Time Key is the one generated at the Map-Server.

Authentication Data is metadata included either in the LISP Encapsulated Control Message header or in a Map-Reply message, to support confidentiality, integrity protection and verification of EID-Prefix authorization. It has three parts. The OTK Authentication Data is the part of the Encapsulated Control Message Authentication Data that contains a One-Time Key. The EID Authentication Data is the part used to verify EID-Prefix authorization. The Packet Authentication Data is the part of the Map-Reply Authentication Data used to protect the integrity of the Map-Reply message itself.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one key per lookup, and three pieces of signed data travel with the lookup: the key itself, the address range the server says is allowed, and a signature over the whole reply.

sections.title: The Threat Model
sections.content:
LISP-SEC addresses the control plane threats described in Sections 3.7 and 3.8 of RFC 7835 that target EID-to-RLOC mappings, including manipulation of Map-Request and Map-Reply messages and malicious ETR EID-Prefix overclaiming. It makes two main assumptions. First, the LISP Mapping System is expected to deliver a Map-Request message to its intended destination ETR as identified by the EID. Second, no on-path attack can be mounted within the LISP Mapping System. How the Mapping System is protected from on-path attacks depends on the Mapping System used and is out of the scope of the memo. While LISP-SEC enables detection of EID-Prefix overclaiming attacks, it assumes that Map-Servers can verify the EID-Prefix authorization at registration time.

According to the threat model of RFC 7835, LISP-SEC assumes that any kind of attack, including on-path attacks, can be mounted outside the boundaries of the LISP Mapping System. An on-path attacker outside the Mapping System can, for example, hijack Map-Request and Map-Reply messages and spoof the identity of a LISP node. Another example of an on-path attack, the overclaiming attack, can be mounted by a malicious ETR by overclaiming the EID-Prefixes for which it is authoritative, so that it can maliciously redirect traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The design assumes the inside of the LISP Mapping System is trustworthy, and that the danger comes from outside it: someone on the path who can alter messages, or a router that lies about which addresses it serves. LISP-SEC is built to catch both.

sections.title: How a Secured Lookup Runs
sections.content:
The security mechanisms of RFC 9301 prevent unauthorized insertion of mapping data by providing origin authentication and integrity protection for the Map-Register and by using the nonce to detect an unsolicited Map-Reply from off-path attackers. LISP-SEC builds on those mechanisms, leveraging the trust relationships among the LISP entities to securely distribute a per-message One-Time Key that provides origin authentication, integrity and anti-replay protection to the mapping data, and that effectively prevents overclaiming attacks.

The processing of the security parameters during a Map-Request and Map-Reply exchange is as follows. For each Map-Request message, a new ITR one-time key is generated and stored at the ITR, and is securely transported to the Map-Server. The Map-Server uses that key to compute an HMAC that protects the integrity of the mapping data known to it, which prevents overclaiming attacks. The Map-Server also derives a new one-time key, the MS one-time key, by applying a key derivation function to the ITR one-time key, and passes that to the ETR. The ETR uses the MS one-time key to compute an HMAC that protects the integrity of the Map-Reply sent to the ITR. Finally, the ITR uses the stored ITR one-time key to verify the integrity of the mapping data provided by both the Map-Server and the ETR, and to verify that no overclaiming attack was mounted along the path between them.

Step by step, the flow is this. The ITR, needing to send a Map-Request, generates and stores a one-time key, which it encrypts and includes in the Encapsulated Control Message that carries the Map-Request to the Map-Resolver. The Map-Resolver decapsulates that message, decrypts the ITR one-time key if needed, and forwards the Map-Request and the key through the Mapping System in a new Encapsulated Control Message, which the Mapping System delivers to the Map-Server identified by the EID destination address. The Map-Server is configured with the location mappings and policy for the ETR responsible for that EID; it finds the longest-match EID-Prefix covering the requested EID and adds that prefix, together with an HMAC computed using the ITR one-time key, to a new Encapsulated Control Message containing the received Map-Request. It then derives the MS one-time key by applying a key derivation function to the ITR one-time key and includes it in the message it uses to forward the Map-Request to the ETR.

If the Map-Server is acting in proxy mode, the ETR takes no part in generating the Map-Reply, and the Map-Server generates the Map-Reply on behalf of the ETR. Otherwise the ETR decrypts the MS one-time key if needed, originates a Map-Reply with the EID-to-RLOC mapping information, computes an HMAC over the whole Map-Reply keyed with the MS one-time key, copies the EID-Prefix authorization data that the Map-Server put in the request into the Map-Reply, and sends the complete Map-Reply to the requesting ITR. The ITR uses its stored ITR one-time key to verify the EID-Prefix authorization data, computes the MS one-time key with the same key derivation function the Map-Server used, and verifies the integrity of the Map-Reply.
sections.plainLanguage: The requester makes a key for this one lookup and hides it as it travels to the server that holds the mapping. That server signs the address range it is willing to vouch for and makes a second key for the router that actually owns the address. The owner signs the whole answer. The requester then checks both signatures, so it can tell that the range really was authorised and that the answer was not altered in transit.

sections.title: The Authentication Data Formats
sections.content:
LISP-SEC metadata associated with a Map-Request is transported within the Encapsulated Control Message that contains the Map-Request, and metadata associated with a Map-Reply is transported within the Map-Reply itself. The HMAC function AUTH-HMAC-SHA-256-128 MUST be supported, and deployments SHOULD use it, except when communicating with older implementations that support only AUTH-HMAC-SHA-1-96.

The Encapsulated Control Message is used with the S-bit set to 1, to indicate that the LISP header includes Authentication Data. The Authentication Data starts with the ECM AD Type, which is 1 for LISP-SEC Authentication Data, followed by the Requested HMAC ID, which is the HMAC algorithm the ITR wants used to protect the mappings. The OTK Length gives the length of the OTK Authentication Data, the Key ID identifies the pre-shared secret shared by an ITR and the Map-Resolver and by the Map-Server and an ETR, and the OTK Wrap ID identifies how the one-time key is wrapped. The one-time key itself is 128 bits long and is preceded by a preamble whose length depends on the wrapping method.

The EID Authentication Data follows. It starts with the EID-AD Length and the KDF ID, which identifies the key derivation function used to derive the MS one-time key, then a record count, the EID HMAC ID identifying the HMAC algorithm used to protect the EID Authentication Data, the mask length, the address family identifier and the EID-Prefix itself, and finally the EID HMAC.

The Map-Reply carries the same EID Authentication Data structure, followed by the Packet Authentication Data: the PKT-AD Length, the PKT HMAC ID, and the PKT HMAC, which is an HMAC of the whole Map-Reply packet, covering everything from the Map-Reply Type field to the PKT HMAC field, including the LISP-SEC Authentication Data. The Map-Reply uses Type 2 with the S-bit set to 1 to indicate that it includes Authentication Data.
sections.plainLanguage: Both messages carry the same three things: which one-time key is in play, the address range the server authorised, and a signature over it. The Map-Reply adds a signature over the whole reply, so nothing in it can be changed unnoticed.

sections.title: Protecting the One-Time Key
sections.content:
Confidentiality and integrity protection for the MS one-time key MUST be provided on the path between the Map-Server and the ETR, either by enabling DTLS between them or by encrypting the key with the pre-shared secret those two share. The same requirement applies to the ITR one-time key on the path between the ITR and the Map-Resolver. To prevent the ETR's overclaiming attacks, the ITR and Map-Resolver pre-shared secret MUST be independent from the Map-Server and ETR pre-shared secret.

The one-time key is wrapped using the algorithm named in the OTK Wrapping ID field, which identifies both the key encryption algorithm used to encrypt the wrapped key and the key derivation function used to derive a per-message encryption key. Implementations MUST support the OTK Wrapping ID AES-KEY-WRAP-128+HKDF-SHA256, which uses HKDF-SHA256 to derive a per-message encryption key and the AES-KEY-WRAP-128 key wrap algorithm to encrypt a 128-bit one-time key. Implementations MUST also support OTK Wrapping NULL-KEY-WRAP-128, which carries an unencrypted 128-bit one-time key with a 64-bit preamble set to zero. If the NULL-KEY-WRAP-128 algorithm is selected and DTLS is not enabled, the Map-Request MUST be dropped and an appropriate log action SHOULD be taken.

The key wrapping process for AES-KEY-WRAP-128+HKDF-SHA256 works as follows. The pre-shared secret used to derive the per-message key is the one identified by the Key ID. The 128-bit per-message encryption key is computed as per-msg-key = KDF(nonce + s + PSK[Key ID]), where the nonce is the value in the Nonce field of the Map-Request and s is the string OTK-Key-Wrap. That per-message key is then used to wrap the one-time key with AES-KEY-WRAP-128. The AES Key Wrap Initialization Value MUST be set to 0xA6A6A6A6A6A6A6A6, and the output of the operation is 192 bits long: the most significant 64 bits are copied into the One-Time Key Preamble field and the 128 least significant bits into the One-Time Key field. When decrypting, the receiver MUST verify that the resulting Initialization Value equals 0xA6A6A6A6A6A6A6A6, and MUST discard the entire message if the verification fails.
sections.plainLanguage: The one-time key itself has to travel safely, because anyone who reads it can forge the signatures. It is either protected by an encrypted connection, or it is wrapped with a key that is derived per message from a shared secret and the request's nonce, so the same wrapped key cannot be replayed.

sections.title: Deployment and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The document extends the LISP control plane of RFC 9301, so its security considerations apply as well. The threat model assumes the LISP Mapping System is working properly and delivers Map-Requests to a Map-Server that is authoritative for the requested EID. It is assumed that the Mapping System ensures the confidentiality of the one-time key and the integrity of the Map-Reply data, but how the Mapping System is secured is out of scope, as is Map-Register security.

The ITR one-time key MUST be generated by a properly seeded pseudo-random or strong random source. If the Map-Server and the ETR are colocated, LISP-SEC does not protect against overclaiming attacks mounted by the ETR, but in that case the ETR is inside the Map-Server's trust boundaries, so those attacks are not part of the threat model. Deployers should weigh how the threat model applies to their particular use case, and if they ignore a recommendation they should make sure the associated risk is understood.

Provisioning of the keys shared between ITR and Map-Resolver pairs and between ETR and Map-Server pairs should be done through an orchestration infrastructure and is out of scope. Both shared keys should be refreshed at periodic intervals to address key aging or an attacker gaining unauthorized access, and they should be unpredictable random values.

An attacker can capture a valid Map-Request or Map-Reply and replay it. Once the ITR has received the original Map-Reply, the pair of nonce and one-time key stored at the ITR is discarded, so a replayed Map-Reply finds no matching pair and is discarded. A replayed Map-Request costs the Map-Server, Map-Resolver and ETR a LISP-SEC computation, equivalent in resources to a valid one, but the attacker gains nothing because the reply is discarded. DTLS SHOULD be used to provide communication privacy and to prevent eavesdropping, tampering or message forgery between the ITR, Map-Resolver, Map-Server and ETR, unless the one-time key is encrypted another way. DTLS has the responder verified by the initiator, which lets an ITR authenticate the Map-Resolver and a Map-Server authenticate the responding ETR. LISP-SEC mitigates denial-of-service risks by protecting the integrity of the Map-Request and Map-Reply messages, authenticating their origin, and preventing malicious ETRs from overclaiming EID-Prefixes that could redirect traffic aimed at a large number of hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things need care in practice: the one-time key has to be generated from a good random source, and the shared secrets between the routers have to be provisioned and rotated. A captured message can be replayed, but the reply it produces is thrown away, so the attacker only costs some computation.
